transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi, Dr. [Name]. I, um... I guess I'm here because things have been getting really weird lately, especially at work. I work as an accounting clerk, just doing bookkeeping and stuff, you know? And I usually have a system, a really good system for keeping everything straight. But lately, I've just been doing these things that... well, they don't make any sense, even to me. Like, the other day, I was supposed to be entering these expense reports, and instead, I found myself lining up all the receipts across the floor of the office. Just, end to end, all the way down the hall. I don't know why I did it, it just felt like they needed to be there. And then there's the calculator. I've started tapping the keys in sets of nine. Always nine. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Over and over. If I get interrupted, I have to start over. It takes up so much time, but I can't seem to stop myself. And... oh, this is the most embarrassing part. I was standing by the copier the other day, and I just stood there with my hands held up in the air. Like, palms out, just frozen. I stood there for I don't know how long, until one of the managers walked by and asked if I was okay. I didn't even realize I was doing it until she said something. It's just... it's really starting to mess with my job, and I'm worried I'm going to get fired if I keep acting so strange.

When you find yourself doing these things—like lining up the receipts or tapping in sets of nine—do you feel an inner urge or anxiety pushing you to do it that you try to resist, or does it feel more like something outside of you is controlling your actions?

I don't... I don't really know how to explain it. It's not like I'm anxious and trying to stop myself, but it's also not like someone else is moving my arms like a puppet, you know? It's more like... well, take the receipts, for example. When I was looking at that stack of expense reports, it just suddenly felt incredibly important, like, fundamentally necessary, that they be laid out exactly like that. It wasn't a thought like, "Oh, I should do this," it was just... an absolute certainty that this was how the world needed to be arranged at that exact moment. And with the calculator, the nines... it's not a compulsion where I'm thinking, "If I don't tap nine times, something bad will happen." It's just that nine is the only number that feels complete right now. If I stop at eight, it's just... wrong. It's physically uncomfortable, like wearing a shirt inside out, but in my brain. And when I was standing by the copier, with my hands up... I wasn't trying to do that, but I also wasn't fighting it. I just sort of... was. I don't know if that makes any sense. It's like my body and my brain are just doing things because they have to be done, but I don't really know why they have to be done. I just know that they do. And it's so frustrating because I used to be so efficient, you know? I could process fifty expense reports in an hour, no problem. But now, I'm lucky if I get through five because I'm too busy making sure the staples are all aligned facing true north or whatever weird thing my brain decides is the most important task of the day. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly.
Have you had any recent medical illnesses, head injuries, neurological problems, or started any new medications or substances around the time these behaviors began?

No, no, nothing like that at all. I mean, I try to take pretty good care of myself, you know? I haven't been sick with anything. Not even a cold or a sniffle. Actually, the last time I was really sick was maybe two years ago, just a mild bug that kept me out of work for a couple of days, but since then, my immune system has been rock solid. I drink a lot of water, I make sure I get my vitamin C, especially because an office environment is basically just a giant petri dish for germs, right? People are always coming in coughing, but I've been totally healthy. 

And definitely no head injuries. I don't play any contact sports or do extreme stuff or anything like that. I mostly just go to work, come home, maybe play some video games or read. I'm not doing anything where I'd hit my head. I haven't been in any car accidents, haven't slipped and fallen. I'm actually pretty careful about that kind of stuff. I always hold the handrail when I go down the stairs at my apartment complex because they get kind of slick, and I definitely don't want to deal with a concussion or a broken arm or anything that would keep me from typing. So, my head is totally fine, physically speaking, anyway. No neurological stuff that I know of. 

And as for medications, no, absolutely nothing. I don't even like taking ibuprofen unless I have a really, really bad headache, which is super rare for me. I just don't like putting stuff in my body if I don't absolutely have to. So no new prescriptions, no weird over-the-counter supplements, and definitely no, like, illegal substances or drugs or anything like that. I don't even drink that much coffee anymore because I thought maybe caffeine was making me a little too wired at my desk, so I switched to green tea a few months ago, well before all this weird receipt and calculator stuff started happening. 

So yeah, there's absolutely nothing new going into my system, no injuries, no sickness... it's just me. Just my brain doing whatever it is it's doing right now, completely out of the blue. Which almost makes it worse, honestly? Because if I had hit my head or started a new pill, at least I'd have a logical reason for why I'm standing like a statue at the copy machine. But there's just... nothing to point to.
Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds other people don't seem to hear, or having any strong beliefs or ideas that others have told you seem strange or unfounded?

Well, it’s funny you bring that up, because... actually, yeah, there has been something like that. I haven't really known how to talk about it because it sounds so crazy when you say it out loud, you know? But lately, sometimes when I’m just sitting alone at my desk—like, usually it happens around 5:15 or 5:30 when most of the office has cleared out and the overhead fluorescent lights are humming that really annoying pitch, and I'm just trying to finish up a reconciliation report or whatever. I'll just be sitting there, completely alone in my cubicle, and out of nowhere, I hear this man's voice. 

And it’s not like a whisper or just a random thought in my head, it’s an actual, physical voice, like someone is standing right over my left shoulder. He says these really specific things. Like the other day, clear as a bell, he just said, "check line seven." And I mean, I was working on a spreadsheet at that exact moment, so I immediately whipped my head around to see who was looking at my monitor. I thought maybe one of the senior auditors had stayed late and was leaning over my partition to check my work. But there was absolutely nobody there. The whole floor was completely empty. I even got up and walked down the row of desks just to be sure, but it was just me.

And it doesn't just happen at work, either. I've been taking this evening class to try and get some more credits, you know, maybe move up from just being a clerk eventually. And when I'm walking home from class—it's usually pretty dark by then, and I take this route where the streetlights are kind of spotty—I'll be walking along, totally by myself, maybe just listening to the cars on the main road a few blocks over, and suddenly I'll hear that exact same guy's voice. He'll say something like, "you missed the sign." 

And I'll stop dead in my tracks on the sidewalk and spin around, looking for whoever is talking to me, or looking for whatever sign he's talking about. I always think someone is walking right behind me. But there's never anyone there. It's just me and the empty street. It's so vivid and loud that I actually check the shadows and the parked cars sometimes, just in case someone is hiding and messing with me. So, yeah, I guess I am hearing a voice that other people don't hear, but it's just so hard to wrap my head around because it sounds so incredibly real. Like, how can my ears physically hear a man speaking when there is absolutely no one around? It just adds to that whole feeling that everything is off right now.
Thinking back, how long ago did you first start noticing these behaviors and the voice—was it weeks ago, or has this been building for several months or longer?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it definitely hasn't just been a few weeks. It’s actually been building for a pretty long time. I'd say it’s been about ten months now? Yeah, ten months sounds exactly right, because I remember exactly what was going on in my life when things first started feeling a little... off. 

That was right around the time I decided I needed to step up my game career-wise. I mean, I only have my high school diploma right now, and I've been working as a bookkeeping clerk, which is fine, you know? It pays the rent, my boss is okay, but I don't want to just be a clerk forever. I want to actually move up in the company, maybe become a full accountant someday. So, ten months ago, I enrolled in these evening accounting courses. And man, let me tell you, trying to juggle a full-time job where I'm staring at spreadsheets and expense reports all day, and then taking the bus straight to a classroom to stare at more numbers and balance sheets until nine at night... it's a lot. It really stretches you thin, going non-stop from 8 AM to almost 10 PM by the time I get home. 

But anyway, that's exactly when all this started. About ten months ago, right when I took on that double load of keeping my bookkeeping job and doing the evening classes. At first, it was just really small things, you know? Like maybe I'd arrange my pencils a little too perfectly before I could start my homework, or I thought I heard someone mumble my name in the hallway at the college when nobody was there. I just brushed it off because I figured I was just tired from the schedule. But over these last ten months, it's just been slowly building and building, creeping up on me day by day, until it turned into... well, into what I was just telling you about, with the calculator nines and the literal voice over my shoulder telling me to check line seven. So yeah, definitely not a sudden thing. It's been a solid ten-month build-up.

During these past ten months, have you noticed any sustained changes in your mood—like feeling unusually depressed, hopeless, or on the flip side, abnormally elevated, euphoric, or irritable—that lasted for a week or more at a time?

Well, yeah, now that you mention it... the elevated or irritable part, I mean. I wouldn't say I've been depressed or hopeless. I'm actually really driven right now. But there are definitely these stretches, usually lasting for a solid week or maybe even two weeks at a time, where I just feel... I don't know, unusually sharp? It's like my brain is just firing on all cylinders, you know? I'll get home from my evening accounting class at 10 PM, and instead of being totally wiped out like a normal person would be after a fourteen-hour day, I'm just buzzing. I feel almost unstoppable. I'll sit down at my little kitchen table with my laptop, and I'll literally map out my entire future in one night. I'm talking five-year, ten-year career plans, calculating exact timelines for when I'll pass the CPA exam, researching which top-tier auditing firms I'm going to run someday, building these massive, complex spreadsheets for my future investment portfolios until like 3 or 4 in the morning. And the crazy thing is, I don't even feel tired the next day at the office. It's this incredible rush, like I'm ten steps ahead of everyone else in the world.

But... the flip side of that, which I guess is what you were asking about with the irritability, is that during those exact same weeks, I get this really intense edge to me. Because my brain is moving so incredibly fast, if anyone interrupts my flow or questions me, it's bad. Like, just the other week, my boss—who is usually a perfectly nice guy, honestly, just a standard manager—he came over to my cubicle to give me a really small correction on an expense report. It was literally just a minor formatting thing. And normally I'd just say 'whoops, my bad' and fix it in two seconds, but instead, I just... I snapped at him. Way, way harder than I meant to. I got incredibly defensive and practically bit his head off about how he was micromanaging me and slowing down my workflow, which is just crazy to say to your boss, right? 

And it happens at the college, too. Just a few days ago, a classmate tried to correct my math on a practice balance sheet during a study group, and I just went off on him, telling him he was dragging me down and that he couldn't see the bigger picture. I always feel terrible about it afterward, but in the moment, I just feel so elevated and fast that even the tiniest correction makes me incredibly irritable. It's like a switch flips and I just can't tolerate anyone being on a slower wavelength than me. So yeah, those weeks definitely happen, and they've been happening more and more over these last ten months.

Do you notice the voice saying things like 'check line seven' and these behaviors like lining up receipts or freezing with your hands up only during those high-energy, irritable weeks, or do they also happen when you're feeling like your normal, even-keeled self?

Well, see, that's the thing that really confuses me about all of this. Because you'd think, right? You'd think it would only happen when I'm running on empty or when my brain is just going a million miles an hour and I'm snapping at people. And I actually kind of tested that theory myself, because I wanted to see if maybe I just needed to force myself to rest and slow down. 

So, there was this stretch recently—maybe for a solid three or four weeks straight—where I really made a point to just be normal. I was sleeping perfectly normally, getting a solid eight hours, no late-night portfolio building, no staying up until 4 AM. I felt totally even-keeled, just completely baseline, not especially energized at all. I was just going to work, doing my bookkeeping, going to my evening class, and actually going to sleep at a reasonable hour. 

But... the weird stuff didn't stop. That's what really threw me. Even during those several weeks when my mood was completely stable and I was resting, I still heard the voice. I'd be sitting there at my cubicle, totally well-rested, drinking my morning coffee, feeling completely fine, and clear as day, that guy would still say 'check line seven' right over my shoulder. And I still felt totally pulled into those number patterns, too. Like, I'd still catch myself staring at the calculator, getting obsessed with the nines, or feeling like I had to line up the receipts perfectly before I could enter them into the ledger, even though I had zero of that intense, buzzing energy. 

I'd just be sitting there, feeling completely calm, but my hands would still freeze up over the keyboard, and I'd still be checking over my shoulder for a guy who wasn't there. So it’s definitely not just when I’m hyped up. It’s like those things—the voice, the patterns, all of it—they just stuck around even when the rest of me went back to normal. Which honestly just makes it even harder to focus on my classes, because I can't just blame it on being overtired or moving too fast anymore, you know? It's just there, no matter how I'm feeling.

Over these past ten months, if you add up all the time, would you say the hyper, irritable weeks have made up more than half of that time, or have there been longer stretches—weeks or months at a time—where your mood was completely normal but the voice and the compulsive behaviors were still going on?

Well, if I really sit down and look at the calendar... I mean, being a numbers guy, I actually try to quantify this stuff in my head, you know? Because I like to have a clear picture of my timeline, especially with how chaotic work and school have been. When I look back at the whole ten months since I started those evening accounting classes... it's honestly mostly been those wired stretches. 

I know I just mentioned that one period where I felt totally normal for a few weeks, and there have definitely been a few other little pockets like that where things kind of settled down for a minute, maybe a few days here or a week there where I could just catch my breath. But if you take all those calm weeks and put them in one column, and put the hyper, overconfident, irritable weeks in another column... that second column is way, way longer. 

It’s definitely been more than half the time. I’d say the vast majority of this whole ten-month period has been spent in that elevated gear. Even when the intensity kind of rises and falls—like, maybe one week I'm just a little edgy at the office and the next week I'm practically rewriting the corporate tax code at 3 AM on my kitchen table—that underlying buzzing feeling is usually there. It's like my engine is just constantly revving, even if I'm not always flooring the gas pedal, if that makes sense. 

So yeah, looking back at the whole picture, the wired, overconfident, and irritable stretches have absolutely taken up way more of this whole period than the calmer stretches. The calm periods are really just the exception. Most of the time, I'm just running incredibly hot, and the voice and the calculator stuff just ride right along with it.

doctor.question: When you find yourself doing these things—like lining up the receipts or tapping in sets of nine—do you feel an inner urge or anxiety pushing you to do it that you try to resist, or does it feel more like something outside of you is controlling your actions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the internal motivation (inner urge/anxiety vs. external control) behind the disorganized behaviors. The symptom profile does not specify the subjective motivation or feeling of control for these specific actions.

patient.answer: I don't... I don't really know how to explain it. It's not like I'm anxious and trying to stop myself, but it's also not like someone else is moving my arms like a puppet, you know? It's more like... well, take the receipts, for example. When I was looking at that stack of expense reports, it just suddenly felt incredibly important, like, fundamentally necessary, that they be laid out exactly like that. It wasn't a thought like, "Oh, I should do this," it was just... an absolute certainty that this was how the world needed to be arranged at that exact moment. And with the calculator, the nines... it's not a compulsion where I'm thinking, "If I don't tap nine times, something bad will happen." It's just that nine is the only number that feels complete right now. If I stop at eight, it's just... wrong. It's physically uncomfortable, like wearing a shirt inside out, but in my brain. And when I was standing by the copier, with my hands up... I wasn't trying to do that, but I also wasn't fighting it. I just sort of... was. I don't know if that makes any sense. It's like my body and my brain are just doing things because they have to be done, but I don't really know why they have to be done. I just know that they do. And it's so frustrating because I used to be so efficient, you know? I could process fifty expense reports in an hour, no problem. But now, I'm lucky if I get through five because I'm too busy making sure the staples are all aligned facing true north or whatever weird thing my brain decides is the most important task of the day. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly.

inference.note: Patient's description of the receipt-lining and tapping rituals lacks the anxiety-driven, ego-dystonic resistance typical of OCD, while the frozen hand-posturing suggests waxy flexibility/catatonic phenomena. This strengthens catatonia-related diagnoses (F20.2, F06.1) and weakens F98.4 (stereotypic movement disorder, more typical in children/developmental contexts) and to a lesser extent F42, though it remains possible given ritualistic behavior.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical, neurological, or substance-related cause that could explain the catatonic-like behaviors (to differentiate a catatonic disorder due to a general medical condition from primary psychotic illness)
doctor.question: Have you had any recent medical illnesses, head injuries, neurological problems, or started any new medications or substances around the time these behaviors began?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical illnesses, head injuries, neurological problems, or new medications/substances to rule out other causes for the symptoms, which is not covered by any specific symptom item in the profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that at all. I mean, I try to take pretty good care of myself, you know? I haven't been sick with anything. Not even a cold or a sniffle. Actually, the last time I was really sick was maybe two years ago, just a mild bug that kept me out of work for a couple of days, but since then, my immune system has been rock solid. I drink a lot of water, I make sure I get my vitamin C, especially because an office environment is basically just a giant petri dish for germs, right? People are always coming in coughing, but I've been totally healthy. 

And definitely no head injuries. I don't play any contact sports or do extreme stuff or anything like that. I mostly just go to work, come home, maybe play some video games or read. I'm not doing anything where I'd hit my head. I haven't been in any car accidents, haven't slipped and fallen. I'm actually pretty careful about that kind of stuff. I always hold the handrail when I go down the stairs at my apartment complex because they get kind of slick, and I definitely don't want to deal with a concussion or a broken arm or anything that would keep me from typing. So, my head is totally fine, physically speaking, anyway. No neurological stuff that I know of. 

And as for medications, no, absolutely nothing. I don't even like taking ibuprofen unless I have a really, really bad headache, which is super rare for me. I just don't like putting stuff in my body if I don't absolutely have to. So no new prescriptions, no weird over-the-counter supplements, and definitely no, like, illegal substances or drugs or anything like that. I don't even drink that much coffee anymore because I thought maybe caffeine was making me a little too wired at my desk, so I switched to green tea a few months ago, well before all this weird receipt and calculator stuff started happening. 

So yeah, there's absolutely nothing new going into my system, no injuries, no sickness... it's just me. Just my brain doing whatever it is it's doing right now, completely out of the blue. Which almost makes it worse, honestly? Because if I had hit my head or started a new pill, at least I'd have a logical reason for why I'm standing like a statue at the copy machine. But there's just... nothing to point to.

inference.note: No medical illness, head injury, neurological disease, or substance/medication exposure identified, making an organic catatonic disorder (F06.1) less likely. The described behaviors (posturing, stereotyped counting, ordering) still fit catatonic features possibly linked to a primary psychotic disorder (F20.2) or reflect 'just right' symmetry/ordering compulsions seen in OCD (F42), so these remain candidates.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations or fixed unusual beliefs that might explain the behaviors, to differentiate catatonic/psychotic process from an obsessive-compulsive disorder
doctor.question: Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds other people don't seem to hear, or having any strong beliefs or ideas that others have told you seem strange or unfounded?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I am alone at my desk or walking home from class, I hear a man's voice say things like 'check line seven' or 'you missed the sign,' clear enough that I look around even though nobody is there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I hear voices or sounds others don't hear, which directly maps to my hallucinations of hearing a man's voice telling me to check lines or that I missed a sign.

patient.answer:
Well, it’s funny you bring that up, because... actually, yeah, there has been something like that. I haven't really known how to talk about it because it sounds so crazy when you say it out loud, you know? But lately, sometimes when I’m just sitting alone at my desk—like, usually it happens around 5:15 or 5:30 when most of the office has cleared out and the overhead fluorescent lights are humming that really annoying pitch, and I'm just trying to finish up a reconciliation report or whatever. I'll just be sitting there, completely alone in my cubicle, and out of nowhere, I hear this man's voice. 

And it’s not like a whisper or just a random thought in my head, it’s an actual, physical voice, like someone is standing right over my left shoulder. He says these really specific things. Like the other day, clear as a bell, he just said, "check line seven." And I mean, I was working on a spreadsheet at that exact moment, so I immediately whipped my head around to see who was looking at my monitor. I thought maybe one of the senior auditors had stayed late and was leaning over my partition to check my work. But there was absolutely nobody there. The whole floor was completely empty. I even got up and walked down the row of desks just to be sure, but it was just me.

And it doesn't just happen at work, either. I've been taking this evening class to try and get some more credits, you know, maybe move up from just being a clerk eventually. And when I'm walking home from class—it's usually pretty dark by then, and I take this route where the streetlights are kind of spotty—I'll be walking along, totally by myself, maybe just listening to the cars on the main road a few blocks over, and suddenly I'll hear that exact same guy's voice. He'll say something like, "you missed the sign." 

And I'll stop dead in my tracks on the sidewalk and spin around, looking for whoever is talking to me, or looking for whatever sign he's talking about. I always think someone is walking right behind me. But there's never anyone there. It's just me and the empty street. It's so vivid and loud that I actually check the shadows and the parked cars sometimes, just in case someone is hiding and messing with me. So, yeah, I guess I am hearing a voice that other people don't hear, but it's just so hard to wrap my head around because it sounds so incredibly real. Like, how can my ears physically hear a man speaking when there is absolutely no one around? It just adds to that whole feeling that everything is off right now.

inference.note: Patient describes true auditory hallucinations (external, third-person voice) and catatonic-like behaviors (posturing, stereotypy) without anxiety-driven resistance typical of OCD; this argues against F42 and supports a psychotic/catatonic schizophrenia picture, so F42 has been ruled out.

doctor.intent: Establish the total duration of these symptoms (voices, unusual behaviors) to assess whether they meet the 6-month threshold needed for a schizophrenia diagnosis
doctor.question: Thinking back, how long ago did you first start noticing these behaviors and the voice—was it weeks ago, or has this been building for several months or longer?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building for about 10 months, since I started the evening accounting courses while keeping my bookkeeping job.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline and how long the symptoms (behaviors and voice) have been building, which corresponds to the overall duration of the illness.

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it definitely hasn't just been a few weeks. It’s actually been building for a pretty long time. I'd say it’s been about ten months now? Yeah, ten months sounds exactly right, because I remember exactly what was going on in my life when things first started feeling a little... off. 

That was right around the time I decided I needed to step up my game career-wise. I mean, I only have my high school diploma right now, and I've been working as a bookkeeping clerk, which is fine, you know? It pays the rent, my boss is okay, but I don't want to just be a clerk forever. I want to actually move up in the company, maybe become a full accountant someday. So, ten months ago, I enrolled in these evening accounting courses. And man, let me tell you, trying to juggle a full-time job where I'm staring at spreadsheets and expense reports all day, and then taking the bus straight to a classroom to stare at more numbers and balance sheets until nine at night... it's a lot. It really stretches you thin, going non-stop from 8 AM to almost 10 PM by the time I get home. 

But anyway, that's exactly when all this started. About ten months ago, right when I took on that double load of keeping my bookkeeping job and doing the evening classes. At first, it was just really small things, you know? Like maybe I'd arrange my pencils a little too perfectly before I could start my homework, or I thought I heard someone mumble my name in the hallway at the college when nobody was there. I just brushed it off because I figured I was just tired from the schedule. But over these last ten months, it's just been slowly building and building, creeping up on me day by day, until it turned into... well, into what I was just telling you about, with the calculator nines and the literal voice over my shoulder telling me to check line seven. So yeah, definitely not a sudden thing. It's been a solid ten-month build-up.

inference.note: The chronic 10-month course, prominent catatonic features (immobility/posturing, stereotyped ritualistic acts), and true auditory hallucinations (audible, localized, command-like) without mood symptoms, substance use, or medical/neurological cause further support schizophrenia, catatonic subtype, and rule out organic or substance-induced etiologies.

doctor.intent: Assess for concurrent mood episode (depressive or manic symptoms) to differentiate schizophrenia from schizoaffective or mood disorder with psychotic features
doctor.question: During these past ten months, have you noticed any sustained changes in your mood—like feeling unusually depressed, hopeless, or on the flip side, abnormally elevated, euphoric, or irritable—that lasted for a week or more at a time?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Some weeks I feel unusually sharp and almost unstoppable, like I can map out my whole future in one night, but then a small correction from my boss or a classmate can make me snap at them harder than I mean to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sustained changes in mood, specifically feeling unusually depressed or abnormally elevated, euphoric, or irritable for a week or more, which matches the symptom of Elevated_Irritable_Mood.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, now that you mention it... the elevated or irritable part, I mean. I wouldn't say I've been depressed or hopeless. I'm actually really driven right now. But there are definitely these stretches, usually lasting for a solid week or maybe even two weeks at a time, where I just feel... I don't know, unusually sharp? It's like my brain is just firing on all cylinders, you know? I'll get home from my evening accounting class at 10 PM, and instead of being totally wiped out like a normal person would be after a fourteen-hour day, I'm just buzzing. I feel almost unstoppable. I'll sit down at my little kitchen table with my laptop, and I'll literally map out my entire future in one night. I'm talking five-year, ten-year career plans, calculating exact timelines for when I'll pass the CPA exam, researching which top-tier auditing firms I'm going to run someday, building these massive, complex spreadsheets for my future investment portfolios until like 3 or 4 in the morning. And the crazy thing is, I don't even feel tired the next day at the office. It's this incredible rush, like I'm ten steps ahead of everyone else in the world.

But... the flip side of that, which I guess is what you were asking about with the irritability, is that during those exact same weeks, I get this really intense edge to me. Because my brain is moving so incredibly fast, if anyone interrupts my flow or questions me, it's bad. Like, just the other week, my boss—who is usually a perfectly nice guy, honestly, just a standard manager—he came over to my cubicle to give me a really small correction on an expense report. It was literally just a minor formatting thing. And normally I'd just say 'whoops, my bad' and fix it in two seconds, but instead, I just... I snapped at him. Way, way harder than I meant to. I got incredibly defensive and practically bit his head off about how he was micromanaging me and slowing down my workflow, which is just crazy to say to your boss, right? 

And it happens at the college, too. Just a few days ago, a classmate tried to correct my math on a practice balance sheet during a study group, and I just went off on him, telling him he was dragging me down and that he couldn't see the bigger picture. I always feel terrible about it afterward, but in the moment, I just feel so elevated and fast that even the tiniest correction makes me incredibly irritable. It's like a switch flips and I just can't tolerate anyone being on a slower wavelength than me. So yeah, those weeks definitely happen, and they've been happening more and more over these last ten months.

inference.note: Added F25.0 and F31.2 given report of distinct week-long periods of elevated/irritable mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, and increased goal-directed activity co-occurring with persistent psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, catatonic posturing, bizarre stereotyped behaviors) over 10 months. Need to clarify whether psychotic symptoms persist outside mood episodes to differentiate schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features versus schizophrenia.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (the voice, the compulsive counting/lining up behaviors, catatonic posturing) occur only during the elevated/irritable mood weeks or also during periods when your mood is normal
doctor.question: Do you notice the voice saying things like 'check line seven' and these behaviors like lining up receipts or freezing with your hands up only during those high-energy, irritable weeks, or do they also happen when you're feeling like your normal, even-keeled self?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch of several weeks when I was sleeping more normally and did not feel especially energized, but I still heard the voice and felt pulled into the number patterns.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (hearing voices, abnormal behaviors) occur outside of the high-energy mood episodes, which directly maps to the requirement of experiencing delusions and hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Well, see, that's the thing that really confuses me about all of this. Because you'd think, right? You'd think it would only happen when I'm running on empty or when my brain is just going a million miles an hour and I'm snapping at people. And I actually kind of tested that theory myself, because I wanted to see if maybe I just needed to force myself to rest and slow down. 

So, there was this stretch recently—maybe for a solid three or four weeks straight—where I really made a point to just be normal. I was sleeping perfectly normally, getting a solid eight hours, no late-night portfolio building, no staying up until 4 AM. I felt totally even-keeled, just completely baseline, not especially energized at all. I was just going to work, doing my bookkeeping, going to my evening class, and actually going to sleep at a reasonable hour. 

But... the weird stuff didn't stop. That's what really threw me. Even during those several weeks when my mood was completely stable and I was resting, I still heard the voice. I'd be sitting there at my cubicle, totally well-rested, drinking my morning coffee, feeling completely fine, and clear as day, that guy would still say 'check line seven' right over my shoulder. And I still felt totally pulled into those number patterns, too. Like, I'd still catch myself staring at the calculator, getting obsessed with the nines, or feeling like I had to line up the receipts perfectly before I could enter them into the ledger, even though I had zero of that intense, buzzing energy. 

I'd just be sitting there, feeling completely calm, but my hands would still freeze up over the keyboard, and I'd still be checking over my shoulder for a guy who wasn't there. So it’s definitely not just when I’m hyped up. It’s like those things—the voice, the patterns, all of it—they just stuck around even when the rest of me went back to normal. Which honestly just makes it even harder to focus on my classes, because I can't just blame it on being overtired or moving too fast anymore, you know? It's just there, no matter how I'm feeling.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, catatonic-like posturing, bizarre stereotyped behaviors) persist independently of mood episodes, confirmed by patient's 3-4 week euthymic period where hallucinations/compulsive patterning continued unabated. This argues against mood disorder with psychotic features (F31.2) since psychosis is not confined to mood episodes, favoring schizoaffective disorder (F25.0) or schizophrenia with catatonic features (F20.2) over bipolar disorder alone.

doctor.intent: Determine whether mood episodes (elevated/irritable periods) have been present for the majority of the total 10-month illness duration, or whether psychotic symptoms have predominated during long stretches without any mood disturbance—key for distinguishing schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Over these past ten months, if you add up all the time, would you say the hyper, irritable weeks have made up more than half of that time, or have there been longer stretches—weeks or months at a time—where your mood was completely normal but the voice and the compulsive behaviors were still going on?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, the wired, overconfident or irritable stretches have taken up more of this whole period than the calmer stretches, even when the intensity rose and fell.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the manic symptoms (hyper, irritable weeks) have been present for more than half of the total 10-month duration of the illness, which directly corresponds to assessing if the mood episode is present for the majority of the total duration.

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and look at the calendar... I mean, being a numbers guy, I actually try to quantify this stuff in my head, you know? Because I like to have a clear picture of my timeline, especially with how chaotic work and school have been. When I look back at the whole ten months since I started those evening accounting classes... it's honestly mostly been those wired stretches. 

I know I just mentioned that one period where I felt totally normal for a few weeks, and there have definitely been a few other little pockets like that where things kind of settled down for a minute, maybe a few days here or a week there where I could just catch my breath. But if you take all those calm weeks and put them in one column, and put the hyper, overconfident, irritable weeks in another column... that second column is way, way longer. 

It’s definitely been more than half the time. I’d say the vast majority of this whole ten-month period has been spent in that elevated gear. Even when the intensity kind of rises and falls—like, maybe one week I'm just a little edgy at the office and the next week I'm practically rewriting the corporate tax code at 3 AM on my kitchen table—that underlying buzzing feeling is usually there. It's like my engine is just constantly revving, even if I'm not always flooring the gas pedal, if that makes sense. 

So yeah, looking back at the whole picture, the wired, overconfident, and irritable stretches have absolutely taken up way more of this whole period than the calmer stretches. The calm periods are really just the exception. Most of the time, I'm just running incredibly hot, and the voice and the calculator stuff just ride right along with it.

inference.note: Patient confirms psychotic symptoms (voice, delusional certainty about behaviors) persisted during a 3-4 week period of documented normal, even-keeled mood, ruling out F20.2 (schizophrenia would not require mood component but the clear mood episode predominance argues against pure schizophrenia) - actually confirms mood episodes occupy majority of illness duration but psychosis persists without mood symptoms for a distinct period, meeting criteria for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0). The manic symptoms (decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, irritability, goal-directed activity) lasting >1 week confirm bipolar-type mood episode rather than depressive, solidifying F25.0 as the sole candidate.
